claims.text: A simulation framework can separately model lattice and electronic heat transport in HfNbTaTiZr.
Explicitly including atomic-scale heterogeneities, 1 wt.% oxygen, and temperature-dependent scattering will improve transport predictions.
The modeled lattice and electronic components will sum to a total conductivity within ±2 W/(K m) of measurement.
The predicted lattice conductivity will differ from previous defect-free estimates by approximately 20–30%.
The target specimen is near-perfect bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing a controlled 1 wt.% oxygen impurity.
Below 200 K, lattice and electronic contributions to heat transport in HfNbTaTiZr are comparable.
Lattice conduction dominates HfNbTaTiZr thermal transport from 300 to 1200 K.
Local bonding variations caused by alloying and oxygen impurities alter force constants.
Local bonding variations alter phonon scattering rates.
Alloy and oxygen heterogeneities influence electronic conduction.
Separately treating phonon and electron scattering while including defects and impurities more accurately captures temperature-dependent conduction.
Prior methods assumed perfect lattices and relied on Debye-temperature or DFT-derived elastic-property approaches.
Measured total conductivity is 10–17 W/(K m) between 300 and 1200 K for the oxygen-containing specimen.
A 20–30% difference from earlier lattice-conductivity estimates constitutes an improvement over those estimates.
Previous analytical and DFT-based estimates did not explicitly decouple lattice and electronic conductivity.
The approach is applicable to HfNbTaTiZr containing up to 1 wt.% oxygen over temperatures from below 200 K to 1200 K.
The approach may not be accurate outside the stated temperature range or at substantially higher impurity levels.
Magnetic-field suppression or modulation can independently isolate the electronic and phonon conductivity components in this alloy.
A total-conductivity error greater than ±2 W/(K m) or a component error greater than approximately 15% in any tested regime will falsify the hypothesis.
